qs.q: During embryological development, the superior parathyroid glands are derived from which of the following structures?
qs.e: Superior parathyroids derive from the 4th pharyngeal pouch, while inferior parathyroids derive from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch. This helps explain why ectopic parathyroid tissue can occasionally be located in the mediastinum.
qs.s: Pituitary + Thyroid & Parathyroid — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: What is the distinctive microscopic feature of oxyphil cells found in the parathyroid glands?
qs.e: Oxyphil cells are large, eosinophilic cells packed with numerous mitochondria which give them their pink color on histology. They appear after puberty and increase with age.
qs.s: Pituitary + Thyroid & Parathyroid — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: During histological examination of a normal adult parathyroid gland, the pathologist notes small polygonal cells with light to dark pink cytoplasm that contain secretory granules. What is the primary function of these predominant cells?
qs.e: Chief cells predominate and serve as the functional cells of the parathyroid gland responsible for PTH synthesis and secretion. Oxyphil cells contain packed mitochondria and have an unknown, likely inactive function.
qs.s: Adrenal Neoplasms and MEN Syndromes — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: During an endocrine pathology seminar, students are reviewing parathyroid gland histology across different age groups. Which statement regarding parathyroid cell populations is accurate?
o: Oxyphil cells increase with age and appear after puberty
Chief cells are largely replaced by stromal fat by age twenty
Water-clear cell hyperplasia is composed of lipid-rich cells
Oxyphil adenomas represent the most common functional tumor
qs.e: Oxyphil cells increase with age and typically appear after puberty, while chief cells remain the predominant functional cell type throughout life. Oxyphil adenomas are actually rare, and chief cells make up most adenomas.
qs.s: Adrenal Neoplasms and MEN Syndromes — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with chronic renal failure presents with persistently low serum calcium and elevated serum phosphate levels. What is the expected compensatory response by the parathyroid glands?
o: Parathyroid gland atrophy with decreased PTH
qs.e: Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs in renal failure as a compensatory mechanism to maintain calcium homeostasis in response to phosphate retention and low active vitamin D. Autonomous PTH overproduction defines primary hyperparathyroidism.
qs.s: Endocrine & Renal Pathology — Must Know Notes — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following cellular components are the predominant and functional cells of the parathyroid gland responsible for synthesizing and secreting parathyroid hormone?
qs.e: Chief cells are the predominant and functional cells of the parathyroid gland, responsible for PTH synthesis and secretion. Oxyphil cells are larger with deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm and have largely unknown or transitional functions.
qs.s: Adrenal Adenoma vs Carcinoma: Diagnostic Criteria — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A pathologist examining a normal parathyroid gland identifies the predominant functional cell type responsible for synthesizing parathyroid hormone. What are the characteristic cytologic features of these cells?
o: Polygonal cells with light to dark pink cytoplasm
Larger cells densely packed with dark mitochondria
Glycogen-rich clear cells with vacuolated borders
Primitive cells devoid of intracellular granules
qs.e: Chief cells are the predominant functional cells of the parathyroid gland, measuring 12-20 μm with light to dark pink polygonal cytoplasm and PTH secretory granules. Oxyphil cells are larger, deeply eosinophilic, and packed with mitochondria.
qs.s: Adrenal Adenoma vs Carcinoma: Illustrated Review — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Parathyroid glands are embryologically derived from
qs.e: Superior parathyroids derive from the 4th pharyngeal pouch, inferior parathyroids from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch (same as thymus). This explains why ectopic parathyroid tissue can be found in the mediastinum alongside ectopic thymic tissue.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The parathyroid glands are small endocrine organs on the posterior thyroid that release PTH to keep blood calcium stable. Their location, blood supply and innervation are key for surgery and for recognizing disease.

sections.p: Each person has 2–4 parathyroid glands, usually four, embedded in the posterior thyroid capsule. They are the main source of parathyroid hormone, the chief regulator of calcium and phosphate balance.
b: Chief cells produce PTH; oxyphil cells increase with age

sections.p: Glands lie behind the thyroid lobes, often at the level of the inferior thyroid pole; superior glands are more constant, inferior glands vary with the thymus and brachial arches.
b: Inferior glands: may be in mediastinum or within thymus

sections.p: Posterior to the thyroid, anterior to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and adjacent to the inferior thyroid artery branches. Their proximity to the nerve makes injury a surgical risk.
b: Recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheoesophageal groove
Inferior thyroid artery supplies both thyroid and parathyroids

sections.p: Primarily from the inferior thyroid artery (branches to inferior glands) and the superior thyroid artery (branches to superior glands). Collateral flow from the thyroid veins helps maintain perfusion.
Parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve travel with the recurrent laryngeal nerve; sympathetic fibers accompany the superior thyroid artery. Autonomic input modulates PTH release.

PTH raises serum calcium by stimulating bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and activation of vitamin D, which increases intestinal calcium absorption. It lowers phosphate by reducing renal reabsorption.
Hyperparathyroidism (primary, secondary, tertiary) and hypoparathyroidism cause dangerous calcium disturbances. Surgical removal or inadvertent devascularisation can lead to permanent hypocalcaemia.
b: Primary hyperparathyroidism: solitary adenoma most common
Secondary hyperparathyroidism: chronic kidney disease, vitamin D deficiency
Tertiary: long‑standing secondary disease with autonomous PTH

t.b: Is calcium high, low, or normal? Guides diagnosis (hyper vs hypo)
Is PTH inappropriately elevated or suppressed? Differentiates cause of calcium abnormality
Is there a focal gland enlargement? Detects adenoma or hyperplasia
Does the gland retain radiotracer? Localises hyperfunctioning tissue

sections.p: Know the typical posterior thyroid location, blood supply from inferior thyroid artery, and that PTH rises when calcium falls. Recognise the three forms of hyperparathyroidism and their labs.
b: Primary: high Ca, high PTH, low phosphate
Secondary: low/normal Ca, high PTH, high phosphate (CKD)
Tertiary: high Ca, very high PTH after long‑standing secondary

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of kidney stones with hypercalcaemia
Acute neck swelling with stridor after thyroid surgery (possible parathyroid injury)

faq.q: Why does low calcium trigger PTH release?
faq.a: Parathyroid chief cells have calcium‑sensing receptors; low extracellular calcium removes inhibition, prompting PTH secretion.
Yes; many patients are discovered incidentally by mild hypercalcaemia on routine labs.

faq.q: What causes hypoparathyroidism in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Post‑surgical removal, extensive neck infection (e.g., TB), or autoimmune destruction are common.
